explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Peter says, “These men are not drunk, as you suppose.” His reason is the clock: “It is only the third hour of the day!” So the proof is that it's still morning, not that it's late at night.
You caught it, baker. Peter's reason is the time of day: “It is only the third hour of the day!” Nothing in his words says it's late at night. The third hour is Peter's whole case.

That's it. Peter quotes Joel, a prophet, and God says, “…I will pour out My Spirit on all people.” Then the list keeps going: sons, daughters, young men, old men, and even servants. God's list has no VIP section.

I see why you'd think it. But in the words Peter quotes from Joel, God says He will pour out His Spirit “…on all people.” Then He names sons and daughters, young men, old men, and menservants and maidservants. Priests aren't named at all.

Kings would be the big names on any guest list, I'll give you that. But in Joel's words, God says “…I will pour out My Spirit on all people.” The ones named are sons and daughters, young men, old men, and menservants and maidservants. No kings, no crowns, no fancy chairs.

Yes, baker, yes, that's true. Joel's words, as Peter quotes them, end with this: “And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” Wonders in the sky come first, but the promise is what lands last. Everyone who calls, saved.

Not this time, friend. Peter's quote from Joel ends with a promise: “And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” The sky signs come before it, but this is the final note. So the statement is true.

Right on. Peter says Jesus “…was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge…” Then he says the crowd, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death. He holds both truths in the same breath, and he doesn't blink.

Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:2), is a name people reach for here. But Peter never names him in this sermon. He says Jesus “…was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge…” The plan belongs to God.

Herod shows up in the story of Jesus' trial (Luke 23:7), so I get the guess. But Peter doesn't name him in this sermon. He says Jesus “…was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge…” The set plan is God's.

That's right, baker. Peter says, “But God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for death to keep Him in its grip.” So the statement is true. Impossible. Death had its grip out and couldn't hold on.

Close, but it's the other way around. Peter says, “But God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for death to keep Him in its grip.” So the statement is true. Death couldn't hold Him.

Yep. David says, “Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell in hope…” That's from Psalm 16, and Peter quotes it. David's heart is glad, his tongue is joining in, and the rest of him is hopeful.
I get it, Hades sounds scary. But David says, “…I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices…” Afraid isn't the word he uses for his heart. Glad is.

Hades isn't a cheerful word, so troubled makes sense. But David says, “Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell in hope…” That comes right after he says God will not abandon his soul to Hades. Troubled isn't the word he uses. Glad is.

explanations.answer: The Christ rising from the dead
explanations.explanation: You got it. Peter says David was a prophet and, “Foreseeing this, David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay.” David's tomb was still right there, so his words pointed to Someone else. Peter says God has raised this Jesus.

explanations.answer: His son Solomon on the throne
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son, did take his throne (1 Kings 2:12), so I see the link. But Peter says David, “Foreseeing this,” spoke about “…the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay.” Peter's point is that the words are about the Christ rising.

Reasonable guess, since it's David's own psalm. But Peter says David died and was buried, and his tomb was still there with them to this day. So David couldn't be describing himself. Peter says David “…spoke about the resurrection of the Christ…”
Not quite, friend. Peter says, “God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses.” Notice the word “all.” He's not a one-man show, because he stood up with the Eleven.
That's right, baker. Peter says, “God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses.” It's “we,” not just “I.” Peter stood up with the Eleven, and he says “all.”

Yes! Peter says, “Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, He has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear.” The “He” is Jesus. Peter has just said God raised this Jesus, so the pieces line up.

Joel is the prophet whose words Peter quotes earlier, so he's fresh in mind. But Joel isn't the One exalted to God's right hand. Peter says that's Jesus, who “…has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit…” Joel spoke the promise, and Jesus poured out what the crowd sees and hears.

David is the big name in this part of the sermon, so I see why he came to mind. But Peter says, “…David did not ascend into heaven…” The One exalted to the right hand of God is Jesus. He's the One who has poured out what the crowd now sees and hears.

There it is. Peter says, “Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!” That's the whole sermon landing in one sentence. And he says it with certainty.

Prophet is a fine title, and David is called one in this very sermon. But Peter's big finish says God has made this Jesus “…both Lord and Christ!” The word is Lord. Peter just quoted David saying, “The Lord said to my Lord…” so Lord is the word he's been building toward.

Priest is a respected title, I'll give you that. But Peter's final words are that God has made this Jesus “…both Lord and Christ!” Lord is what he says. He puts it right at the end, where nobody can miss it.

That's the one. The people were cut to the heart, and they asked Peter and the other apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” Their question is about what to do next. Peter replies in the very next verse.

explanations.answer: Brothers why did no one warn us
explanations.explanation: That question sounds natural for a crowd that's been cut to the heart. But the text doesn't have them say it. They ask, “Brothers, what shall we do?” That's a question about what to do next.

Peter has just said Jesus was exalted to the right hand of God, so the question isn't far off. But the crowd doesn't ask it. They're cut to the heart and ask, “Brothers, what shall we do?” It's a question about what to do, and Peter answers it right away.

Yes, baker, yes! Peter says, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins…” Notice “…every one of you…” Nobody gets a pass, and nobody gets left out.

Fasting and sacrifices might be what a crowd in Jerusalem expects to hear. But Peter doesn't say that. He says, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ…” Those are the two things.

Praying is good, and the believers do it later in this very passage. But it's not what Peter tells this crowd to do. He says, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins…” Those are the two things: repent and be baptized.

That's right. Peter says to be baptized “…in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins…” He also says they'll receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Forgiveness and a gift in the same sentence is a lot of good news.
Plenty of people carry fears, and I've carried a few myself. But Peter's words are “…for the forgiveness of your sins…” That's what the baptism in Jesus' name is for.

Doubts, friend? I had plenty back in that junk drawer I lived in for years. But Peter doesn't say doubts. He says to be baptized “…in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins…” Sins is the word, and it's a big one.

Not quite, baker. Peter says, “This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off…” Then he adds, “…to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.” That reaches way past the crowd that day.

You've got it. Peter says, “This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off—to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.” The promise isn't only for the crowd. It goes out to their children and to those who are far off.

That's not how it went. The text says, “Those who embraced his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day.” Three thousand. That's not a handful, that's a stadium.
That's right, baker. The text says, “…about three thousand were added to the believers that day.” That is a LOT of people added in a single day. I'd lose count somewhere around forty.

That's the word. The text says, “A sense of awe came over everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs.” Awe is that hush when you realize something bigger than you is happening. Everyone felt it, and nobody was left out.

Doubt is a common feeling when big things happen, but it's not what the text says. It says, “A sense of awe came over everyone…” And the apostles were performing many wonders and signs while it happened.

Anger, huh? I get that way over a jammed oven door, so I understand the guess. But the text says, “A sense of awe came over everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs.” The word is awe, and it came over everyone.

Yep. The text says, “Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need.” They'd just heard the good news, and they shared with whoever needed it. I'd have been checking my own shelves for spare chocolate chips.
That's not what the text says. It says, “Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need.” So the statement is true. They sold what they had and shared it.

explanations.answer: Adds to their number those being saved
explanations.explanation: You got it. The text says, “And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.” Daily, not just on Pentecost. The believers are praising God, and He keeps adding people.

explanations.answer: Opens prison doors for the apostles
explanations.explanation: That happens in a different place, when an angel of the Lord opens the prison doors (Acts 5:19). It isn't what verse 47 says. Here the text says, “And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.”

explanations.answer: Sends them out to other nations
explanations.explanation: That's not what this verse says. It says the believers were praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. Then: “And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.” That's what the Lord does, day after day.
